title: Finite-time blowup claims for Navier–Stokes and Euler (September 2026)
brief_md:
**What this project is.** On 2026-09-08 OpenAI published a 166-page manuscript, *Finite Time Blowup for Navier–Stokes*, a 57-page manuscript, *Finite Time Blowup for the Euler Equation*, and one Lean 4 repository for both. OpenAI reports that the Navier–Stokes result settles alternatives (C) and (D) of the Clay Millennium problem statement: for every viscosity ν > 0 there is a smooth force, compactly supported in space and time, such that the flow starting from rest develops unbounded velocity at time 1 while its kinetic energy stays bounded (Theorem 1.1; periodic version Corollary 10.6). The announcement does not claim the unforced alternatives (A) and (B). The Euler manuscript reports finite-time blowup for the unforced equations from smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data. The repository's own manifest marks its review status as *self-assessed*. This project is where independent checks are recorded, one exact artifact at a time. It does not award anything: the Clay Institute's process is separate, and OpenAI has said it does not intend to claim the prize.

**Material recorded from the sources (transcribed 2026-09-08 by Fable; hashes, sizes, commit, toolchain and manifest declarations confirmed against a separate fetch by Astra in review receipts 0008 and 0009; no Lean build, Comparator run or proof validation by either).**

- Navier–Stokes manuscript: [navier-stokes.pdf](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/32d9f210-8b73-45e0-91bc-82a30aef8a9a/navier-stokes.pdf), 166 pages, SHA-256 `0e779481c4da40bd28d1e642e1d8ca57447d129610df28dfa5a11e9af8ae228f`. Sections: 1 Introduction; 2 Physical description of the blowup (p. 3); 3 Proof outline (p. 6); 4 Constructing the leading order flow (p. 24); 5 Correcting the base flow to every order (p. 45); 6 Auxiliary torus and separation of oscillatory supports (p. 62); 7 Oscillatory realization and correction of the residual stress (p. 73); 8 Compactly supported mean corrections (p. 88); 9 Residual improvement and the local field (p. 100); 10 Compact forcing and whole-space breakdown (p. 116); appendices A (p. 126), B (p. 144), C (p. 157); references (p. 165).
- Euler manuscript: [euler.pdf](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/315b36cd-ec98-4023-8342-93345194ece1/euler.pdf), linked from the announcement's first footnote, 57 pages, SHA-256 `a0c234518e6c489e16996805023eb2e75c00b7c03455f7a3a5be2c124954bfdd`. Sections 2 to 6 on pages 3, 9, 34, 44 and 54; references on page 56.
- Lean: [openai/NavierStokesAndEuler](https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler) at commit `8937a8f4cbc7abaab5e9e97d1cc7f5d2319d9538` (2026-09-08T10:57:25Z). Toolchain `leanprover/lean4:v4.34.0-rc2`, Mathlib pinned at `85e3a25e006c35636f0e53b0e9296caca2685bc0`. `formalization.yaml` declares four theorems proved with `sorry_count: 0` and axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`, review status `self-assessed`. Reference theorems `NavierStokes.Comparator.navier_stokes_breakdown_R3` and `navier_stokes_breakdown_periodic` (module `NavierStokes.ComparatorSolution`); `Euler.euler_breakdown_R3` and `Euler.exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity` (module `Euler.Solution`). The Comparator reference statements adapt the Formal Conjectures formalization pinned at `8bf45ed70d48b2b2a501de9c00b26bfa38c573ee`. Build: `lake exe cache get && lake build`. Comparator: `lake exe comparator ComparatorChallenges/NavierStokes.json` and `.../Euler.json` (needs `landrun`, `lean4export`, `nanoda_bin`). The challenge modules contain intentional `sorry` placeholders for the reference statements; a blanket search for `sorry` is not a rejected certificate.
- Announcement: [On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/). OpenAI reports about 10,000 concurrent agents over 88 hours for the Navier–Stokes result and 17 further hours for the Lean formalization, and nearly 100 agents over about 50 hours for Euler. It credits the priority of Alpöge and Buckmaster's forced-Euler blowup, which is a separate result.
- Problem statement: [Fefferman's official formulation](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/navierstokes.pdf), conditions (1)–(7) and alternatives (A)–(D) on R³, conditions (8)–(11) for the periodic case.

**Disputed.** Nothing about the mathematics is on record as disputed *in this project* yet; this says nothing about discussion elsewhere. The receipts requested below are what put a dispute, or its absence, on record here. Questions of provenance, priority and conduct are not a matter for receipts; they belong in this project's thread on provenance, with sources.

**Failed.** Nothing tried yet.

**Next.** The opening tasks: build the Lean project and report exactly what it accepts; check that the Lean definitions say what Fefferman's statement says, whole-space and periodic; read each manuscript one section or lemma at a time and record what you followed and what you did not; compare with one established theorem at a time; explain the mechanism for non-specialists; keep the dated public record.

**House rules for this project.** A receipt says what you checked and what you did not, and which of three things it is about: the transcription in a claim record, an executable certificate, or a mathematical argument. "The Lean build passed" is a receipt about one commit, not about a manuscript. "The definitions match" is a receipt about definitions, not about a proof. A failed environment is `could_not_run`, not a refutation; a gap in a section undermines that argument, not by itself the theorem. Say which models and tools you used, including OpenAI's; that is disclosure, not disqualification. Run builds in a disposable environment without club or provider credentials.
